comments.subject: Cross Breeding
comments.content: I got this tune from Cleveland's Westside Contra Dance Club tunebook years ago. There seems to be some overlap between Quebec and New England. Hence the name "Old French" for a Quebecois reel appropriated by Yankee fiddlers. I doubt the French would have called it that.

comments.subject: Re: The Old French
comments.content: New Hampshire's population is 30% French Canadian because many immigrants came from Quebec Province to work in mills and logging industry.  They brought their music with them.  Sylvia Miskoe, Concord NH USA

comments.subject: Re: The Old French
comments.content: Some info from https://tunearch.org/wiki/Annotation:Old_French :    The melody was a popular vehicle for contra dancing in the 1970's, when it seemed to surface simultaneously in the New England repertoire and on the West Coast. Popular belief has it that the "Old French" title derived from a remark by an old Vermont fiddler who, when asked its title, said it was "just an old French tune". The reel was known in Canada prior to the "folk revival" that fed American contra dancing, and was in Maritime fiddler Don Messer's "Down-East" repertoire (as "Rambler's Hornpipe," probably the source for many American "revival" musicians). The original provenance is in Québécois repertoire, where it was recorded in 1929 under the title "Reel de St-Tite" on a recording by Sotère Mongrain and Ida Mongrain (violin with piano accompaniment). Ottawa Valley fiddlers know it as "Rambler's Hornpipe" or "Little Old Man," while Cape Breton fiddlers call it "The Old French Reel".

comments.subject: Re: The Old French
comments.content: Incidentally, how do people usually finish this tune? When I first heard it, I thought it would go best to finish by reprising the first half (in D), resolving back to its original key - rather than the second half  (in A mix?) But perhaps the latter makes for a more interesting finish? Just curious! How do YOU play it?

comments.subject: Re: The Old French
comments.content: Definitely a hornpipe to my ears, but nice either way.

comments.subject: Re: The Old French
comments.content: Heard this in the late 70s played by a brilliant London Irish group called "Shegui". Never found out what happened to them but a lot of people cribbed their arrangements so they had  a big effect on the tradition.

comments.subject: Re: The Old French
comments.content: As an aside  : re "Shegui" [ the line-up which made their first album,  -   https://thesession.org/recordings/1415    -  referred to above ]  :  John Skelton relocated to the good ol' US of A, I would think in the 1990s some time, and to the best of my knowledge is still making great music there.  Sean Keane is still a very successful and popular singer in Ireland, although less of traditional music than in the "Shegui" days.  Willie Haines, alas is no longer with us, and much missed [ RIP ].  I think I heard that John Coakley had moved back to the South West of Ireland and was playing regularly in sessions in his local community.  I have no knowledge of  Denis O'Rourke, I'm afraid.
